Exeter's population increased by around 12,900 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 130,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Exeter increased by 11.0%, from around 117,800 in 2011 to around 130,700 in 2021.

The population here increased by a greater percentage than the overall population of the South West (7.8%), and by a greater percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Exeter was home to around 19.8 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 17.9 in 2011. This area was among the top 25% most densely populated English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was higher in Exeter than across the South West

Median age stable in Exeter

The latest census data also show that the average (median) age remained 35 years in Exeter between the last two censuses.

This area had the second-lowest average (median) age in the South West (behind Bristol) and a lower average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by around 2,800 (an increase of 14.9%), while the number of residents aged 4 years and under fell by just over 850 (12.8% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 0.6 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Family in Exeter

The percentage of households including a couple with dependent children increased in Exeter, but fell across the South West.

In Exeter, the percentage of households including a couple with dependent children rose from 16.4% in 2011 to 17.0% in 2021. During the same period, the regional percentage fell from 18.6% to 17.9%.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Exeter fell from 17.7% to 17.5%, while the percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children increased from 4.8% to 4.9%.

The percentage of households including a couple with dependent children in Exeter increased by 0.7 percentage points

Changing relationships in Exeter

Exeter saw the South West's second-largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership (from 9.4% in 2011 to 8.8% in 2021).

Across the region, only Bristol saw a greater fall in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership (from 8.2% to 7.4%).

Across the South West, the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 9.8% to 10.1%, while the percentage in nearby East Devon increased from 9.8% to 10.4%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership in Exeter decreased by 0.6 percentage points

Rise in private renting

Exeter saw the South West's joint second-largest percentage-point rise (alongside Gloucester) in the proportion of privately-rented homes (from 21.0% in 2011 to 24.9% in 2021).

Across the region, only Isles of Scilly saw a greater rise in the percentage of privately-rented homes (from 29.7% to 36.6%).

Because of its small size, comparisons to Isles of Scilly should be made with caution.

Every local authority area across the South West saw a rise in the percentage of privately-rented homes, as the regional percentage grew from 17.1% to 19.7%.

Private renting in Exeter increased by 3.9 percentage points

Disability in Exeter

Exeter saw the South West's largest percentage-point rise in the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little (from 10.2% in 2011 to 11.6% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Mid Devon saw the South West's next largest increase in the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little (from 9.6% in 2011 to 10.9% in 2021).

Every local authority area across the South West saw a rise in the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little, as the regional proportion grew from 10.1% to 10.8%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a little in Exeter increased by 1.4 percentage points

National identity in Exeter

Exeter saw the South West's joint third-largest percentage-point rise (alongside Bristol) in the proportion of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK (from 7.6% in 2011 to 10.2% in 2021).

Across the region, only Swindon (from 8.6% to 13.6%) and Sedgemoor (from 3.0% to 5.9%) saw a greater increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK.

Across the South West, the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK increased from 4.4% to 6.1%, while the percentage in nearby East Devon increased from 2.2% to 3.3%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Exeter increased by 2.6 percentage points

Exeter residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 107,200 Exeter residents said they were born in England. This represented 82.0% of the local population. The figure has risen from around 101,200 in 2011, which at the time represented 85.9% of Exeter's population.

Wales was the next most represented, with just under 2,100 Exeter residents reporting this country of birth (1.6%). This figure was up from around 1,800 in 2011, which at the time also represented 1.6% of the population of Exeter.

The number of Exeter residents born in Poland rose from around 1,300 in 2011 (1.1% of the local population) to around 2,000 in 2021 (1.5%).

In 2021, 82.0% of Exeter residents reported their country of birth as England

Unpaid care in Exeter

In 2021, 4.8% of Exeter residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 7.3% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Exeter (2.5 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the South West (2.8 percentage points, from 7.5% to 4.7%). Across England, the proportion fell by 2.8 percentage points, from 7.2% to 4.4%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Exeter decreased by 2.5 percentage points

Religion in Exeter

In 2021, 48.5% of Exeter residents reported having "No religion", making it the most common response in this local authority area (up from 34.7% in 2011). Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the South West, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 29.3% to 44.1%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 40.0% of people in Exeter described themselves as Christian (down from 53.9%), while 7.4% did not state their religion (down from 8.1% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Read the bulletin Religion, England and Wales: Census 2021.

In 2021, 48.5% of usual residents in Exeter reported having "No religion"

Change in employment

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in Exeter (3.5 percentage points) than in nearby East Devon (1.1 percentage points).

In Exeter, the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) decreased from 53.9% in 2011 to 50.5% in 2021. During the same period, the percentage in nearby East Devon decreased from 52.4% to 51.3%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) in Exeter fell from 2.8% to 1.9%, while the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were retired (economically inactive) decreased from 19.0% to 18.5%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Exeter decreased by 3.5 percentage points

Fewer adults working long hours

In 2021, 8.8% of Exeter residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked over 49 hours per week. This figure decreased from 10.3% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in eight people (12.4%) said they worked 15 hours or less per week, compared with 12.1% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 56.4% to 58.0%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked over 49 hours per week was greater across the South West (2.5 percentage points, from 13.3% to 10.8%) than in Exeter (1.5 percentage points). Across England, the percentage fell by 2.2 percentage points, from 13.3% to 11.1%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults in employment who worked 49 hours or more in Exeter decreased by 1.5 percentage points

Health in Exeter

In 2021, 48.8% of Exeter residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 46.6% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 34.5% to 33.5%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Exeter residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.2% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 4.2% to 4.0%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in Exeter increased by 2.2 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Exeter

In 2021, 4.9% of Exeter residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 3.9% in 2011. The 1.0 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the South West, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 2.0% to 2.8%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 90.3% of people in Exeter identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 93.1% in 2011), while 2.5% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 1.6% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.8% in 2011 to 1.4% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.

In 2021, 4.9% of usual residents in Exeter identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category
